summary: Depth-first rabbithole dossier for $near and $nearSphere; source-anchored research pack.

facts.text: **F3. Firestore's MongoDB-compatibility layer documents `$near` only, with no `$nearSphere` at all**, requires "at least one 2dsphere index", uses meters, and adds that "`$near` isn't supported in aggregation queries". <https://docs.cloud.google.com/firestore/mongodb-compatibility/docs/geo-query>

25. Amazon DocumentDB implements both operators, but documents only the GeoJSON form: `$near` there requires a `2dsphere` index, takes `$geometry`, and measures `$maxDistance` / `$minDistance` in metres. The legacy coordinate-pair form, the `2d` index path, and radian units — the parts of `$near`/`$nearSphere` that date to 2010–2011 — are absent from DocumentDB's reference. Code written against MongoDB's legacy syntax will not port. — <https://docs.aws.amazon.com/documentdb/latest/devguide/near.html>, <https://docs.aws.amazon.com/documentdb/latest/devguide/nearSphere.html>

**D3 — Does `$nearSphere` accept legacy coordinates on a 2dsphere index?** The Geospatial Queries overview tabulates `$nearSphere` with legacy coordinates as 2d-index-only (<https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/geospatial-queries/>). The `$nearSphere` reference page contains a worked example headed "2dsphere Index" that runs `$nearSphere: [-73.9667, 40.78]` with `$minDistance` against a 2dsphere index, and states `$minDistance` for legacy coordinates "is available only if the query uses the 2dsphere index" (<https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v5.0/reference/operator/query/nearSphere.md>). The referen

6. `2dsphere` indexes support spherical queries only; `2d` indexes support planar queries and *some* spherical queries, and the manual warns that using a `2d` index for spherical queries "can return incorrect results or errors" — for example `2d` indexes do not support spherical queries that wrap around the poles. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/geospatial-queries/ 7. The distinction between the operators is stated most explicitly in the `$geoNear` reference: `spherical: true` uses "`$nearSphere` semantics and calculates distances using spherical geometry", while `spherical: false` uses

**A4. Adding `.sort()` to a `$near` query silently destroys the distance ordering and adds a blocking sort.** "The `$near` operator sorts documents by distance… If you use the `sort()` method in your query, MongoDB performs a second sort operation, re-ordering the matching documents. When querying large collections, this can negatively affect query performance." <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.0/reference/operator/query/near.md> <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/nearSphere/>

**D1. There is no index-selection escape hatch for `$near` in a `find()`.** MongoDB requires the `key` option to disambiguate when a collection has multiple geospatial indexes — but that option exists only on the `$geoNear` aggregation stage. `find()` with `$near` has no equivalent. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/geospatial/restrictions.md>

7. `$minDistance` with legacy coordinates is available only when the index is `2dsphere`; it is unavailable with a `2d` index. `$maxDistance` is available for either index type. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/nearSphere/

6. `$minDistance` was introduced in MongoDB 2.6, and at that time was available only when the query used a `2dsphere` index. — <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/docs/v2.6/source/reference/operator/query/nearSphere.txt>, <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/mindistance/>

17. Both operators sort results implicitly from nearest to farthest. Adding an explicit `sort()` causes MongoDB to perform a *second* sort, re-ordering the results and degrading performance on large collections; `$geoWithin` is the documented alternative when ordering is not needed. — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/near/>

20. After each interval the annulus width adapts against a target band of 300–600 results: `if (lastIntervalStats.numResultsReturned < 300) _boundsIncrement *= 2; else if (lastIntervalStats.numResultsReturned > 600) _boundsIncrement /= 2;`. This is the mechanism that keeps a `$near` scan efficient in both dense cities and empty ocean. — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/master/src/mongo/db/exec/classic/geo_near.cpp

21. Expansion terminates when the searched region reaches the outer bound: "The search is finished if we searched at least once and all the way to the edge", with `kMaxEarthDistanceInMeters` capping expansion at half the Earth's circumference. An unbounded `$near` therefore has a definite end, not an unbounded one. — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/master/src/mongo/db/exec/classic/geo_near.cpp

15. The ordering invariant is bought by buffering: "Results in each interval are buffered fully before being returned to ensure that ordering is preserved." A document is only emitted once every document that could be closer has been seen. — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/master/src/mongo/db/exec/classic/near.h

16. The stage is responsible for de-duplication, because the child index scan of an annulus can return the same document more than once: "The child stage may return duplicate documents, so it is the responsibility of NearStage to deduplicate. Every document in `_resultBuffer` is kept track of in `_seenDocuments`." A `RecordIdDeduplicator` holds the seen ids. — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/master/src/mongo/db/exec/classic/near.h

- **Source independence.** The quality gate asked for different hosts, and five were used, but three of them (`mongodb.com`, `raw.githubusercontent.com` serving `mongodb/mongo`, `jira.mongodb.org`) are all MongoDB Inc. properties. Only the Mongoose issue and the Amazon DocumentDB documentation are genuinely third-party, and neither is a deep account of the mechanism. The gate is met on host count and on the presence of a disconfirming class of evidence (claims 33–36), but not on full organisational independence — no independent reimplementation or peer-reviewed analysis of MongoDB's expanding-

31. MongoDB's spherical model treats Earth as a sphere of equatorial radius 6,378.1 km. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/geospatial/2d/calculate-distances/ 32. Great-circle distance formulas applied to geodetic latitude and longitude on Earth "are accurate to within about 0.5%", and "any single formula for distance on the Earth is only guaranteed correct within 0.5%" relative to the WGS84 ellipsoid. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great-circle_distance 33. Consequence (derived from claims 31 and 32): a `$nearSphere`/`$maxDistance` boundary is accurate to roughly h

**B5. MongoDB's radian conversion uses the *equatorial* radius: 3,963.2 mi / 6,378.1 km.** <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/calculate-distances-using-spherical-geometry-with-2d-geospatial-indexes/> Third-party guides commonly instruct `km / 6371` (the *mean* radius), a ~0.11% systematic disagreement at the boundary of `$maxDistance`; e.g. <https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-03-31-mongodb-nearsphere-spherical/view>. Both are spherical approximations: neither matches a WGS84 ellipsoidal geodesic, so `$nearSphere` distances should not be treated as survey-grade.

This report covers only the `find()`-level query predicate operators `$near` and `$nearSphere`: where they silently return wrong or incomplete results, where they error, how their distance units and geometry model change under the index type, and where the documentation contradicts itself or other implementations.

The `$geoNear` aggregation stage, the removed `geoNear` command, `$geoWithin`, `$geoIntersects`, `$centerSphere`, GeoJSON parsing, and the 2d / 2dsphere index types are **out of scope** and appear only where a claim about `$near` / `$nearSphere` cannot be stated without them.

**A1. A document whose location field is missing, `null`, or an empty array is silently excluded from every `$near` / `$nearSphere` result — never an error.** 2dsphere indexes are *always* sparse and MongoDB ignores the `sparse` option on creation; "If an existing or newly inserted document does not contain a 2dsphere index field (or the field is `null` or an empty array), MongoDB does not add an entry for the document to the index." <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/geospatial/2dsphere.md>

**C6. The error string `$geoNear, $near, and $nearSphere are not allowed in this context` also surfaces outside query composition — in rule-evaluated Atlas App Services / GraphQL request paths**, where the same query succeeds over a direct driver connection. MongoDB staff attribute this to App Services rule evaluation being unable to support these operators. <https://www.mongodb.com/community/forums/t/geonear-near-and-nearsphere-are-not-allowed-in-this-context/174746>

**E2. The implicit 100-document limit on `$near` was removed in 2.7.5.** SERVER-14515, "Remove default limit from geoNear operations": "The default limit interacts badly with other cursor features, and is no longer needed with progressive 2D near search." The ticket explicitly cites broken interactions with `skip`/`limit` and with `$nearSphere` + map/reduce. Resolution: Done, fix version 2.7.5. <https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-14515> See disagreement D2 — the docs still assert the limit.

**F1. Azure DocumentDB (MongoDB vCore) does *not* enforce the index requirement.** "The `$geoNear`, `$near`, and `$nearSphere` stages don't have strict index requirements, so these queries wouldn't fail if an index is missing." Code that relies on a missing-index error as a guard is portable in one direction only. <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/mongodb/vcore/geospatial-support>

1. `$near` (query predicate operator), MongoDB Manual v8.0 — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.0/reference/operator/query/near.md> 2. `$nearSphere` (query predicate operator), MongoDB Manual (current) — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/nearSphere/> 3. `$nearSphere`, MongoDB Manual v5.0 (archived) — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v5.0/reference/operator/query/nearSphere.md> 4. `$nearSphere`, MongoDB Manual v4.4 (archived; sharded-collection note) — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v4.4/reference/operator/query/nearSphere.md> 5. `$maxDistance`, MongoDB Manual (current) —

13. Starting in MongoDB 8.0, `$near`, `$nearSphere`, and `$geoNear` validate that the type of the specified GeoJSON point is `Point`; any other input type returns an error. — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/near/>, <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/nearSphere/>

18. The operators differ only in geometry: `$near` on a `2d` index measures distance on a flat surface, while `$nearSphere` uses spherical (great-circle) geometry. MongoDB warns that using a `2d` index for spherical data can return incorrect results or an error — for example, `2d` indexes do not support spherical queries that wrap around the poles — and recommends a `2dsphere` index for longitude/latitude data. — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/geospatial/2d/query/proximity-flat-surface/>, <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/calculate-distances-using-sph

23. `$near` and `$nearSphere` cannot be used on time series collections; only the `$geoNear` aggregation stage is supported there, against `2dsphere` indexes. — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/geospatial-queries/>

**U3 — The 100-document default limit on `2d` `$near` queries.** MongoDB 2.4 and 2.6 documentation both state that a `$near`/`$nearSphere` query using a `2d` index returns at most 100 documents by default (<https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/docs/v2.4/source/reference/operator/query/near.txt>, <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/docs/v2.6/source/reference/operator/query/nearSphere.txt>). The current reference and 2d-index pages do not mention this limit at all (<https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/near/>, <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/

27. Starting in MongoDB 8.0, `$near`, `$nearSphere` and `$geoNear` validate that the supplied GeoJSON type is exactly `Point`. Any other type is an error. Before 8.0 this was not enforced at the operator boundary. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.0/reference/operator/query/near.md

28. Neither operator works on time series collections at all: "You can't use `$near` and `$nearSphere` operators on time series collections." Only the `$geoNear` stage against a `2dsphere` index is supported there, and it must specify `key` and must not use `query`. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-limitations.md

- **Sharded collections.** Older community guidance states that a `geoNear` find on a `2d` index is unsupported in a sharded cluster (https://groups.google.com/g/mongodb-user/c/xTy5IJVLW_o/m/xGvz20DO6yIJ). The current manual's sharding restrictions and geospatial index restrictions pages list no such prohibition for `$near`/`$nearSphere` — only that a geospatial index cannot be the shard key (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/limits.md, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/geospatial/restrictions.md). This report covers only the two proximity query predicate operators `$near` and `$nearSphere`: how they are invoked, which index each needs, distance units, sort and execution behaviour, where they are forbidden, portability across MongoDB-compatible engines, and the accuracy envelope of the distance they compute. `$geoNear`, `$geoWithin`, `$geoIntersects`, `$centerSphere`, and the 2d/2dsphere index types themselves are referenced only where a claim about `$near`/`$nearSphere` cannot be stated without them; they are separate frontier items and are not assessed here.

10. With a GeoJSON point, `$maxDistance` and `$minDistance` are in **meters** for both operators. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.0/reference/operator/query/near/ and https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.0/reference/operator/query/nearsphere/ 11. With legacy coordinate pairs, the manual specifies **radians**: the `$near` source text reads "you can use the *optional* `$maxDistance` specification to limit the `$near` results by distance in *radians*", and the syntax block is `{ $near: [ <x>, <y> ], $maxDistance: <distance in radians> }`. This wording is identical in the v4.2 branch and in `master`.

21. `$near`/`$nearSphere` cannot be combined with another operator or command that needs a different special index; the documented example is that `$near` cannot be combined with `$text`. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.0/reference/operator/query/near/ 22. `$near` and `$nearSphere` are Match Execution operators and are **not permitted in aggregation pipelines** (i.e. not usable inside `$match`). — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.0/reference/operator/query/near/ and https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.0/reference/operator/query/nearsphere/ 23. Claim 22 has a large second-order blast radius, becau

**D3. `unable to find index for $geoNear query` is the planner error users see for a `$near` predicate with no usable geo index** — including cases where a 2dsphere index exists but is not usable by the plan, e.g. under `readConcern: "majority"` before the fix for SERVER-20260 (SERVER-20261, MongoDB 3.1.7). <https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-20261>

29. A geospatial index can never cover a query, so a `$near` query always fetches documents; the index alone cannot satisfy it. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/geospatial/restrictions.md

**Three gaps closed cross-report:** the 100-document limit (edge-cases' SERVER-14515 closes what three passes left open — though the docs sentence is still stale and uncorrected); sharded collections (mechanism's open question, settled at 4.0 by the other three); and `$nearSphere` + legacy coords on a `2dsphere` index (practice's worked example plus mechanism's index-conversion claim beat the overview table).

**Seven contradictions preserved side by side.** The load-bearing one is D1 — legacy `$maxDistance` units, where three current first-party MongoDB pages say radians, coordinate units, and metres respectively. All four passes hit it independently; none closed it. The union narrows it (10 radians > a full turn, so the `$maxDistance` page's own example can't be radians; and the radians→metres conversion branch is commented "Hack for nearSphere") but that's inference, not sourced fact. D2 — `$minDistance` on a `2d` index — is visible *only* in the union: history alone found the 4.0 release note cl

**C2. If an `$or` contains a near clause, it may contain nothing else.** "$or supports geospatial clauses. However, if you use a near clause (`$near` or `$nearSphere`), `$or` cannot contain any other clauses. Using `$or` with a single clause has the same effect as omitting the `$or` operator." Non-near geo clauses such as `$geoIntersects` are fine inside a multi-clause `$or`. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/or.md> Corroborated independently by Firestore's MongoDB-compatibility layer, which also documents that `$near` "can't be used with the `$not` or `$nor` operat

**C3. `$near` / `$nearSphere` cannot be combined with another operator that requires its own special index — `$text` is the named example.** <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.0/reference/operator/query/near.md>

**C4. Starting in MongoDB 8.0, the GeoJSON argument must have `type: "Point"`; any other GeoJSON type returns an error.** Code that passed a `Polygon` or `LineString` to `$near` on 7.0 and earlier becomes a hard failure on upgrade. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.0/reference/operator/query/near.md>

**D2 — Does `$near` still return only the first 100 results?** The current and v4.4 `$maxDistance` pages both state: "The operation returns the first 100 results, unless you modify the query with the `cursor.limit()` method." (<https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/maxdistance.md>, <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v4.4/reference/operator/query/maxDistance.md>). SERVER-14515 removed that default in 2.7.5, explicitly because it "interacts badly with other cursor features" (<https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-14515>). The engineering ticket is the stronger evidence and the

**D5 — Whether a missing index is an error is implementation-defined.** MongoDB documents `$near` as *requiring* a geospatial index and surfaces `unable to find index for $geoNear query`; Azure DocumentDB documents the opposite (F1). Neither party acknowledges the other. Portability assumptions built on either behavior are unsafe.

22. `$or` supports geospatial clauses, but if a near clause (`$near` or `$nearSphere`) is used, `$or` cannot contain any other clause. — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/or/>

12. `2d` indexes do not support spherical queries that wrap the poles, and the manual warns that using a `2d` index for spherical queries "can return incorrect results or errors". This is the concrete failure boundary of claim 9's `$nearSphere` + `2d` cell. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/geospatial-queries/

32. `$geoNear` must be the first pipeline stage, and a `$near` predicate is not permitted inside `$geoNear`'s own `query` field — so the escape hatch from claim 24 cannot be nested back into itself. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/geoNear/

34. Completeness has also broken. SERVER-14039: `$nearSphere` with a `2d` index plus `skip(m)` and `limit(n)` returned `m` fewer documents than expected, and zero when `m == n`. Affected 2.6.3, fixed in 2.6.4; `2dsphere` indexes were not affected. The cause was a miscount that ignored already-skipped documents when sizing the result set. This is direct evidence that the `2d`/`2dsphere` execution paths are separate code with separate defects. — https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-14039

- **Legacy default result cap.** Older MongoDB documentation described legacy `$near` returning at most 100 documents when no `limit()` was given. No such statement appears in the 8.x pages consulted, and the archived v4.4 page could not be retrieved in a usable form. Whether the cap was removed or merely undocumented is unverified.

**D5. Very complex indexed geometry can make writes fail, not reads.** 2dsphere key generation is capped by `indexMaxNumGeneratedKeysPerDocument`, default 100,000 keys per document; an operation needing more fails. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/geospatial/restrictions.md>

30. A geospatial index cannot be a shard key, though a geospatial index may exist on a sharded collection under a different shard key. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/geospatial/restrictions.md

**Saturation: saturated on the documentary record, zero coverage on behaviour.** No server was run in any pass, and every remaining open question is one the docs demonstrably cannot answer. One session against a live server with both index types would close D1, D2, D3, D4 and the stale-limit sentence together. More reading closes none of them.

MongoDB 2.6 introduced stronger validation of geospatial queries — options and GeoJSON specifications are checked and an invalid query errors, where prior versions tolerated or ignored invalid specifications. It also deprecated `$uniqueDocs` and stopped returning duplicate results, and shipped `2dsphere` index version 2. — <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/docs/v2.6/source/release-notes/2.6-compatibility.txt>, <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/docs/v2.6/source/release-notes/2.6.txt>

1. **Radians versus coordinate units for legacy `$near`.** The manual labels legacy-form `$maxDistance` on `$near` as radians (claim 11) and lists `$near` among the radians-taking operators (claim 13), yet `$geoNear` states that `$near` semantics on a `2d` index use *planar* geometry (claim 7). A radian is an angular measure and sits oddly on a planar computation over arbitrary coordinate values. **Quality gate: met.** Claims draw on six independent hosts — `mongodb.com/docs` (current + archived v4.4/v5.0/v8.0 manuals), `jira.mongodb.org` (primary engineering tickets), `mongodb.com/community`, `learn.microsoft.com` (Azure DocumentDB), `docs.aws.amazon.com` (Amazon DocumentDB), and `docs.cloud.google.com` (Firestore MongoDB-compatibility). The last three are deliberately adversarial: they are independent reimplementations whose divergence from MongoDB is disconfirming evidence for any claim that a `$near` behavior is intrinsic rather than MongoDB-specific.

Historical: a compound *multikey* 2dsphere index made `$near` return results ordered by the non-geospatial index field instead of by distance.** SERVER-13687, "Results of `$near` query on compound multi-key 2dsphere index not sorted by distance", triggered by index shapes such as `{ "address.uppercase": 1, "address.location": "2dsphere" }`. Affected 2.6.0 and 2.6.1; fixed in 2.6.2. The fix made the plan enumerator assign the mandatory `$geoNear` predicate before applying multikey index rules. <https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-13687> This is the canonical demonstration that `$near`'

33. The "sorted by distance" guarantee is an implementation property, not a structural one, and it has broken. SERVER-13687: on a compound `2dsphere` index that had become multikey, `$near` results were returned ordered by the other index field instead of by distance. Affected 2.6.0–2.6.1, fixed in 2.6.2 by making the planner assign the mandatory `$geonear` predicate before applying multikey index rules. — https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-13687

5. `$near` with a legacy coordinate pair requires a `2d` index, takes `$maxDistance` in **radians**, and has no `$minDistance`. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.0/reference/operator/query/near.md

8. Longitude is listed first and must be in `[-180, 180]`; latitude is second and must be in `[-90, 90]`. These are inclusive bounds. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.0/reference/operator/query/near.md

The operator does not by itself decide the geometry model; the pair (operator, index) does. `$near` + GeoJSON + `2dsphere` is spherical. `$near` + legacy + `2d` is **flat**. `$nearSphere` + GeoJSON + `2dsphere` is spherical. `$nearSphere` + legacy + `2d` is **spherical**. So the single cell where the two operators genuinely diverge is legacy coordinates on a `2d` index. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/geospatial-queries/

14. `NearStage` runs a four-state machine: `Initializing`, `Buffering`, `Advancing`, `Finished`. — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/master/src/mongo/db/exec/classic/near.h

17. Two concrete implementations exist: `GeoNear2DStage` ("Implementation of GeoNear on top of a 2D index") and `GeoNear2DSphereStage` ("Implementation of GeoNear on top of a 2DSphere (S2) index"). 18. The first annulus width is derived from local data density, not from a fixed constant. The S2 estimator reasons: "Assuming cell size at current level is d and data is even distributed, the distance between two nearest points are at least d. The following circle with radius of 3 * d covers PI * 9 * d^2, giving at most 30 documents." The 2D path likewise records "We expand the radius by 3 times to give a reasonable starting search area." — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/master/src/mongo/db/exec/classic/geo_near.cpp
